title: Morphological Determinants of Intracellular Membrane Compartments
text:
The interior of a human cell is organized through a series of chemically and morphologically distinct membrane-
enclosed compartments, the organelles. The proposed research aims to address how these compartments are
structured and how their interactions are governed by protein condensates that form through phase separation.
Understanding the basic mechanisms that organize the early secretory pathway is critical for interpreting how
disruptions in intracellular architecture contribute to diseases such as neurodegeneration and cancer.

title: Development of B-cell-based vaccine for Glioblastoma
text:
Immunotherapy is a promising approach to treat glioblastoma patients, yet its efficacy so far has
been very limited. Our work provides an opportunity to explore the B-cell-based vaccine as
immunotherapy to treat deadly tumors, including glioblastoma. Our approach utilizes 4-1BBL+ B
cells as a cellular platform to promote anti-tumor immunity.

title: Closing the loop with an automatic referral population and summarization system
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because it improves the quality of care and patient
outcomes during care transitions. The new and improved health information technology solutions proposed in
this project can facilitate an integrated multi-disciplinary approach to improving care transitions by defragmenting
information, improving communication, and assuring the care team has access to reliable and complete health
information that may be located in other care settings or disparate systems. The proposed research is also
relevant to the part of the NLM’s strategic plan that focuses on enabling interoperability of clinical systems and
meaningful use of electronic health records, and effective translation of new knowledge into practice.

title: CDK6-dependent metabolic reprogramming in KSHV pathogenesis
text:
Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV) is the etiological agent of Kaposi's sarcoma
(KS), the leading cancer in AIDS patients afflicting the skin and the mucosa of the oral cavity. We
will uncover new mechanisms by which KSHV manipulates key metabolic enzymes via protein
phosphorylation, thereby reprogramming cellular metabolism to support viral persistence and
tumorigenesis. Our project will reveal cellular molecules that can be targeted to thwart KSHV
pathogenesis.

title: Disrupting the Prostate Tumor Microenvironment in African American Men to Promote Response to Immuno-Modulatory Therapy
text: Gaps in population-based outcomes remain prevalent in prostate cancer leading to large variations in incidence and clinical prognosis, with men of African ancestry (AAM) experiencing the highest burden of these differences. Emerging evidence suggests that there are significant immune-oncologic differences in the prostate tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) of AAM compared to men of European ancestry (EAM). This proposal seeks to functionally characterize the TIME differences within heterogeneous populations and determine the effect on response to immune-modulators, thus opening avenues to identify new therapeutic approaches to improve outcomes in men with PCa.

title: Effect of Iron Deprivation on H. pylori-induced Gastric Carcinogenesis
text:
PPG PROJECT 1 NARRATIVE
These collaborative studies will define bacterial and host factors that influence gastric cancer within the context
of iron deficiency. Such findings will help to identify H. pylori-infected persons at high risk for gastric cancer,
who thereby warrant therapy.

title: Biostatistics and Informatics Core
text: The Biostatistics and Informatics Core is a newly formed Core to support the central aims of the University of Washington (UW) Cystic Fibrosis (CF) Research and Translation Center (CFRTC). It is formed under a continuity of leadership and out of services that have been a cornerstone of the CFRTC by providing novel design, analytics and quantitative methods and analytics. With the advent of big data in CF, a new bioinformatics component has been added to the Core focused on applying cutting-edge computational methods to analyze “omics” data. The Core leaders bring services, expertise, and a long history of collaboration with CF researchers, especially in diabetes, pancreatic function and highly effect CF transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) modulator therapy. Further, the Core has a strong training component for CF researchers and clinicians. The Core establishment is an acknowledgement of the increasing complexity of translational and basic research in CF and the need for a dedicated resource to provide integrated analytic support to the UW CFRTC research base. The services focus on biostatistical support, study design, epidemiologic methods, comparative effectiveness and cost analyses, ancillary study enrichment, and novel bioinformatics services to guide and assist the research base with analysis of large- scale omics data. The Core aims are consistent with the overall CFRTC: 1) adapt biostatistical methods and outcomes to the post-HEMT era, 2) enhance understanding of non-pulmonary comorbidities in CF and improve decision making and policy through effectiveness and cost analytics, 3) and perform state-of-the art bioinformatics on human and animal data to understand pathophysiology and clinical manifestations of CF post-HEMT. The Core will foster collaboration across the CFRTC through training and sharing existing databases that enable ancillary analyses.

title: Dissecting the role of common and rare risk variants in IKZF1 in B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia predisposition and pathogenesis
text:
Inherited genetic variation plays an increasingly recognized role in the pathogenesis of B-cell acute
lymphoblastic leukemia, the most common childhood cancer. Genetic association studies, including my prior
work, have identified numerous risk variants, but the precise mechanisms by which these variants drive
leukemogenesis are unknown and remain a critical unmet need. This proposal aims to close the
variant-to-function gap by systematically dissecting the molecular consequences of germline predisposing
variation at the IKZF1 gene locus, with the ultimate goal to design mechanism-based therapies to reduce the
global burden of a leading cause of childhood mortality.

title: Cell Metabolism
text: The Cell Metabolism (CMB) Core provides access to mass spectrometry strategies and related methodologies for the study of cellular metabolism. This core was founded using philanthropic funding (2013-2019) and appears in this renewal as a CCSG Shared Resource for the first time. The inclusion of the CMB Core is motivated by a maturation in the technologies with which to interrogate cellular metabolism, growing expertise within the group, increasing demand for metabolomic analyses among investigators, and the need to incorporate this key aspect of cancer biology into the Center’s strategic framework for leading pioneering research. The laboratory operates a technology platform that is being leveraged by basic, translational, and clinical research groups across MSK. The Core provides a reservoir of knowledge in the development and implementation of cutting-edge analytical strategies with experienced scientific staff who assist in leveraging these analytical capabilities. The Core offers routine metabolomic and lipidomic profiling, provides advice on study design, sample preparation, and the choice of experimental approaches. The Core also assists extensively with data analysis and interpretation. Since 2020, the Core Director has also served as the Program Co-Director for an NIH R25 Research Education Program that provides training in current metabolomics and lipidomics strategies for trainees at MSK and neighboring NYC metro area institutions. The CMB Core has contributed to at least 65 publications in the reporting period, including many in high-impact journals.

title: TDP-43 Proteinopathy in ALS-FTD: Mechanism, Target Validation and Biomarker
text:
The discovery of loss of TDP-43 splicing repression occurring in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) and
Fronto-temporal Dementia (FTD) provided the opportunity to test whether such function is compromised during
early stage of disease, develop prognostic test, and to design therapies to treat this illness, currently without
effective treatment. We recently discovered that loss of TDP-43 function occurs in pre-symptomatic ALS-FTD
patients, providing rationale to develop a prognostic test for sporadic ALS as well as for developing a
therapeutic strategy to complement loss of this TDP-43 function for ALS.

title: Immunoengineering Durable Control of HIV Replication
text: Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) with CCR5Δ32 hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) can replace the hematopoietic system with HIV-resistant blood cells and has been the only curative therapy for HIV to date.1-3 While an important proof-of-concept, allo-HSCT for HIV cure is hindered by the scarcity of CCR5Δ32 donors and a toxicity profile that restricts its application to a subset of people living with HIV (PLWH) with hematological malignancies. Gene therapy presents a highly promising approach that with significantly enhanced safety and accessibility by modifying a patient’s own (autologous) HSCs to confer HIV-resistance. HSC gene therapy approaches continue to evolve to improve CCR5-editing efficiency, eliminate the need for laborious and costly ex vivo gene editing procedures, and avoid toxic chemotherapy conditioning regimens. Our proposal addresses these challenges by direct modification of HSCs in vivo to inactivate CCR5 for HIV- resistance and enrichment of edited cells using novel CD45 epitope editing methods to protect them from CD45- specific immunotherapy. We anticipate our in vivo gene editing strategy will surpass previous approaches in editing efficiency, safety, and accessibility, making it suitable for widespread application including among healthy PLWH and low- and middle-income (LMIC) countries where HIV is most prevalent. We will harness our in vivo gene therapy to enhance HIV protection and elimination by sustained delivery of promising anti-HIV effectors, including the synergistic combination of eCD4-Ig and 10-1074, as well as the Brec1 recombinase that will excise proviruses. In our well-established NHP model of suppressed HIV infection, we have a breadth of data demonstrating the feasibility of our approach including efficient CCR5 gene editing in HSCs, robust depletion of CD45+ cells using anti-CD45 antibodies, HSC modification to express eCD4-Ig and bNAbs, and in vivo delivery of the Brec1 recombinase to excise proviruses. Our in vivo gene therapy approach will use our latest generation helper dependent adenoviral (HDAd) vector, which we have demonstrated to safely and efficiently modify HSCs in vivo. Overall, our goal is to apply next-generation in vivo CCR5 editing and selection in combination with anti-HIV effector delivery to achieve a safe and accessible HIV cure.

title: Targeting Protein Arginine Methyltransferases to Eradicate Acute Myeloid Leukemia
text:
Overall outcome for patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) remains unfavorable. The limited applicability
of allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) as well as the rise of the immunotherapy era
highlights a pressing need to develop novel immune-stimulating drugs for AML eradication. To address this
challenge, herein, we will determine whether targeting PRMT9 promotes a sustained leukemia-eliminating
immunity and assess whether a PRMT9 inhibitor combined with an immune checkpoint inhibitor eliminates AML
cells in-vivo.

title: Smartphone-based community screening for eye disease in rural India
text: Anterior eye segment diseases such as cataract, refractive error, and corneal opacity are leading causes of global blindness, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. In order to improve access to anterior eye disease screenings in rural settings, our project aims to develop and validate a smartphone-based, community health worker-led platform to screen patients for common anterior eye diseases. We will compare performance of ophthalmologists’ remote grading of smartphone screening data to the gold standard of in-person eye camp exams; we will also compare performance of a machine learning algorithm trained using smartphone screening data and images to the gold standard of in-person eye exams. By enabling community-based screening with remote or automated interpretation, this approach could ultimately expand access to timely eye care for rural populations, including in the United States, while reducing dependence on scarce specialist resources.

title: Exploiting FLVCR1-mediated choline transport in acute myeloid leukemia
text:
Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a challenging blood cancer, and the disease subtype harboring the
CBFA2T3-GLIS2 fusion protein is associated with dismal outcomes under standard therapies. This project will
investigate how the choline transporter FLVCR1 supports the survival of CBFA2T3-GLIS2 AML and whether its
inhibition can selectively suppress cancer cells while sparing normal blood stem cells. These studies could
lead to new precision treatment strategies for this aggressive AML and reveal broadly applicable principles for
targeting choline uptake in cancer.

title: The neuroprotective role of DPSC EVs overexpressing microRNA-22-3p
text:
Retinal ischemia causes severe vision loss with significant inflammatory and apoptotic
consequences in the retina. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) derived from bone mesenchymal stem
cells (BMSCs) improved retinal inflammation and apoptosis, which is attributable to microRNAs
(miRs) within EV cargo. This proposal will determine the anti-apoptotic and anti-inflammatory
effect of dental pulp stem cell (DPSC) EVs, a distinct source of MSCs, and the efficacy of DPSC
EVs that overexpress miRNA-22-3p in retinal ischemia.

title: Functional analysis of ZnT8 in islet cells and its application to diabetes
text:
Genetic studies have established the association between a membrane transport protein termed ZnT8 and
susceptibility to diabetes. The focus of this proposal is to study ZnT8 functions using a combination of
biochemical and cell biological techniques. The study is expected to provide mechanistic insights of ZnT8
function in pancreatic islet cells to help design new therapeutic strategies for preventing and treating diabetes.

title: Determining the role of amygdalostriatal transition zone circuits in associative learning and motivated behaviors
text:
Normal responses to environmental stimuli are disrupted in many neuropsychiatric disorders, leading to
damaging behavioral outcomes. This study will determine the role of the amygdalostriatal transition zone (ASt)
- an almost completely unstudied structure - in mediating learned behavioral responses to stimuli that predict
rewards or punishments. The proposed research project will increase our knowledge of the fundamental neural
mechanisms underlying associative learning and motivated behaviors, and could identify ASt circuits as novel
targets of interest for psychological disorders such as anxiety, depression, and post-traumatic stress disorder.

title: Reactivating regulatory programs for regeneration
text:
Human cardiac injury, such as a heart attack, leads to irreparable damage and life-long heart complications. This
proposal explores the gene regulatory controls that dictate heart repair in a regenerative organism, the zebrafish,
which will reveal candidates for reprogramming human-derived cardioids to elicit a regenerative response.
Distinctive synergies between multiomics approaches and diverse cardiac models will make feasible a
longstanding goal of regenerative medicine: reactivating the latent capacity of the human heart to regenerate
post-injury.

title: LUMICKS C-Trap optical tweezer/microfluidics/confocal system
text:
The Center for Mechanical Excitability seeks to purchase a correlative optical tweezers-superresolution
microscopy instrument to address the critical need for combined single molecule force and fluorescence analysis
throughout the UChicago campus and the Chicagoland region. This instrument will significantly enhance studies
on important biomolecular mechanisms in health and disease, including hearing and balance, cell migration,
nucleic acid conformation, synaptic formation, as well as pathological conditions related to cancer, deafness and
Parkinson’s. These studies, which will only be possible with this new instrument, will provide critical insight for
the development of new molecular-based drugs and therapies. Importantly, there is no equivalent instrument
available as a shared instrument at The University of Chicago, or the greater Chicago area.

title: Biophysical studies of viral membrane fusion proteins
text:
Influenza hemagglutinin is a model system for studying the mechanism by which enveloped viruses fuse
membranes during entry into cells. The proposed research will lead to a better understanding of the
mechanism of influenza and SARS-CoV-2 entry, specifically, and class-I viral membrane fusion in general. We
will also biophysically evaluate avian influenza strains, as well as human pandemic strains that originated in
birds to determine the mechanistic features that avian strains must acquire to infect humans.
